author: fester
body: Stage 1. Re-derives, from the IR text alone, the four properties a well-formed chapter must have: every name is bound by something, every application agrees with the function type its callee carries, every constructor is applied to the payload types its own sum type declares, and every match arm binds sub-patterns at the constructor's field types.

author: fester
body: Names a body may legitimately mention: the locals in scope, the chapter's own definitions, its constructors, and the builtins the language supplies. A name resolving to none of these is bound by nothing.

author: fester
body: A double underscore prefix is a compiler intrinsic by the language's own naming rule, so it resolves without appearing in any table.

author: fester
body: Literals carry no type on the wire, and a literal's type is whatever its context admits, so their type is absent rather than wrong. Absent compares as undecided.

author: fester
body: One node does not carry its own type and it is not marked on the wire. A list expression's type field holds the ELEMENT type: the IR builds it with the element type and the compiler's own accessor wraps it in ListTy on the way out. Read straight off the wire, `(list-expr (elems ...) int-default)` says int-default where the node's type is List Integer, and the rechecker reported every list argument in the tree as a type mismatch until this was wrapped. Any consumer of this wire has the same trap waiting, and nothing in the wire format announces it.

author: fester
body: A constructor pattern is checked against the scrutinee type it carries: the constructor must be one of that type's, and each sub-pattern must bind at the field type the constructor declares. Builtin List patterns (Cons, Nil) carry a ListTy rather than a SumTy and are not re-checkable from the wire, so they are undecided rather than wrong.

author: fester
body: A sum type declared in the chapter under test arrives inlined as a SumTy carrying its constructors. A sum type reached by CITATION does not: it arrives as `(ctd "Maybe" (args ...))`, a bare name and its type arguments, and every Maybe, Result and Either in the tree is that shape. Reading only the inlined form left constructor checking covering same-chapter types and nothing else, which the first tree sweep showed as UNSUPPORTED on every `Just` and `None`.

author: fester
body: The constructors are on the wire, in the chapter's `(type-defs ...)` section, so the name is resolved there. Field types are surface ATypeExpr rather than CodexType and carry the declaration's own type parameters, so ARITY is checked and the payload types are answered UNSUPPORTED unless the field is a bare parameter reference this declaration's arguments can substitute.

author: fester
body: Multi-field constructors are curried, so the parameter types are gathered down the arrow chain until it arrives at the sum.

author: fester
body: An application is checked against the type its own callee carries: the argument must have the parameter type, and the application's result type must be the callee's return type. Nothing here consults a signature from outside the wire, so what is being asked is whether the IR agrees with itself.

author: fester
body: `__narrow` is how the guide says a plain Integer is asked into a bounded slot: an assertion checked at runtime, trapping if violated. So the argument's static type is EXPECTED to differ from the bounded parameter, and the difference is the point rather than a finding. Stage 2 already skips a narrowed argument at the same slot and stage 1 did not, which reported every explicit narrow in the tree as a type mismatch.

author: fester
body: The exemption is only for an INTEGER parameter. A narrow handed to a parameter of any other type is still a mismatch and is still reported, which is what keeps this from being a hole shaped like a fix.

author: fester
body: A do-bind is in scope for the statements that follow it, not for its own value expression.
